questions.q: In the cancer metabolism context of this course, aerobic glycolysis refers to which of the following?
options: A kinase in the MAPK signalling pathway; an early event in the serrated colorectal cancer pathway.
The first step of energy production: glucose is broken down into pyruvate without using oxygen.
Splitting sugar into lactate even when oxygen is plentiful — the pathway cancer cells prefer.
The study of the chemical composition of exhaled breath, used to look inside the body.
questions.why: Aerobic glycolysis is the Warburg effect: cancer cells still convert glycolytic pyruvate into lactate even when oxygen is plentiful. The numbers on the slide are that in proliferating cancer cells about 85% of pyruvate goes to lactate and only about 5% enters the mitochondria, so aerobic glycolysis nets only about 4 ATP, whereas a normal cell with oxygen makes about 36 ATP. The easily confused items are glycolysis itself (the first step that cuts glucose into pyruvate), BRAF (a kinase on the MAPK pathway) and breathomics (analysing the chemical composition of exhaled breath).

questions.q: What is the core concept of an antibody-drug conjugate (ADC)?
options: Using the antibody as a delivery vehicle, carrying a toxic drug only to the place it recognises.
A branched linker that carries two drugs at once.
An ADC that carries two drugs on the same antibody.
The poisonous component on an ADC that does the killing.
questions.why: An ADC has three parts: the antibody that recognises the antigen, the linker that joins the two, and the payload that does the killing. The reasoning is practical: chemotherapeutic drugs kill normal cells too, so the drug is packaged as an antibody plus a toxin, letting the toxin be released only where the antibody finds its antigen; his example is trastuzumab-deruxtecan (a HER2 ADC). A branched linker splits the linker into two arms, a dual-payload ADC carries two drugs on one antibody, and a cytotoxic payload is the poisonous component that does the killing — all three are merely components of an ADC.

questions.q: In this course's signalling pathway and colorectal cancer model, which of the following correctly describes BRAF?
options: Its stuck mutant form drives many cancers, including colorectal and pancreatic cancer.
A signalling kinase downstream of the receptor, the main transmitter of HER2 signalling.
The growth factor receptor at the very top of the RAS chain. Blocking it is a standard anticancer drug strategy.
A kinase in the MAPK signalling pathway; an early event in the serrated colorectal cancer pathway.
questions.why: BRAF is a kinase downstream in the MAPK pathway, normally controlled by upstream RAS signalling; once it mutates it sends out a continuous growth signal by itself, and the cell no longer needs the upstream switch. In his colorectal cancer model the adenoma pathway runs APC early, KRAS in the middle and p53 late, while the serrated pathway has BRAF early; the two routes converge in the end, both ending in high-MSI adenomas. K-Ras is the stuck mutant driver gene, PI3K is the kinase that carries HER2 signalling downwards, and EGFR sits at the very top of the chain.

questions.q: Which of the following does a branched linker refer to?
options: Using the antibody as a delivery vehicle, carrying a toxic drug only to the place it recognises.
A branched linker that carries two drugs at once.
The poisonous component on an ADC that does the killing.
The umbrella term for topoisomerase inhibitor payloads of the DXd type.
questions.why: An ordinary ADC linker is linear, with the antibody at one end and one drug at the other; changing it to a branched linker forks the linker into two arms, each carrying one drug: usually a topoisomerase inhibitor plus an inhibitor of the DNA damage response (for example an ATM blocker), used to counter the resistance that a single payload breeds. The cost is a bigger molecule and a lower drug payload, so it remains a research-stage design rather than an approved standard practice. The ADC itself is the antibody used as a delivery vehicle, the cytotoxic payload is the poison that does the killing, and deruxtecan is the umbrella term for payloads of the DXd type.

questions.q: The technique that studies the chemical composition of exhaled breath to look inside the body is called ____ in English.
options: Metabolomics
NMR
Breathomics
Metabolite fingerprint
questions.why: Gas can be 'sniffed' for disease. His lecture one slides describe the whole workflow: the tumour microenvironment (cancer cells, alveolar cells, T cells, neutrophils, macrophages, fibroblasts, cytokines, metabolites) constantly gives off volatile organic compounds, which are collected on solid-phase microextraction fibres and then analysed by GC/MS. The clinical value is that it is entirely non-invasive: a single breath can screen for lung and gastric cancer, with no needle and no radiation; but false positives and the consistency of the breath-collection method have to be watched. Metabolomics is the study of all the small molecules in a sample, NMR is used to work out the shape of molecules in solution, and a metabolite fingerprint is the pattern of small molecules that makes one sample differ from another.

questions.q: Why does he stress that a patient's having cancer cannot be concluded from a single CEA value?
options: Because in this course CEA is positioned as a clinical trial surrogate endpoint and a circulating surrogate marker, used to track tumour burden in place of repeated scans; to use it in place of the true endpoint, you must first show that it moves in step with the true endpoint.
The study of the chemical composition of exhaled breath, used to look inside the body.
Compressing thousands of measurements into a few axes so that cells can be plotted as points.
The step curve showing how patients' survival probability changes over time.
questions.why: CEA stands for carcinoembryonic antigen. It is present at very low levels in normal adult tissue but is expressed heavily in the foetal gut and on colorectal cancer cells, so a rise in blood CEA is often taken as a clue to tumour burden. He positions CEA as a circulating surrogate marker, a far cheaper stand-in for a CT scan that lets a trial avoid scanning every patient every few weeks. He also warns that a surrogate is only a surrogate and cannot on its own establish a diagnosis. The chemical composition of exhaled breath, the dimensionality reduction of PCA and the Kaplan-Meier step curve have nothing to do with this reading.

questions.q: On a Kaplan-Meier curve, those little tick marks represent patients who are ____.
options: median overall survival
surrogate endpoints
prognostic biomarker
censored
questions.why: Those little tick marks on a Kaplan-Meier curve are the censored patients: they left the study, were lost to follow-up, or were still alive with no event at the time the curve was drawn. A censored patient contributes no negative information — at that moment they still have 'no event' — so the curve stays flat at the point where they drop out instead of stepping down. Reading a KM curve is the first-tier question he asks in every lecture, and interpreting censoring is a compulsory part of it. Median overall survival is the endpoint measure reported in trials, surrogate endpoints means substituting a cheap marker for the true endpoint, and a prognostic biomarker answers the natural history of the disease.

questions.q: What is Cetuximab's role in this course, and under what condition does it work?
options: The growth factor receptor at the very top of the RAS chain. Blocking it is a standard anticancer drug strategy.
An anti-EGFR antibody; effective in K-Ras wild-type rectal cancer, ineffective in patients with K-Ras mutations.
Its stuck mutant form drives many cancers, including colorectal and pancreatic cancer.
A RAS inhibitor; median overall survival 13.2 months, against 6.7 months for chemotherapy.
questions.why: Cetuximab binds EGFR and blocks the growth signals it receives, on the condition that the tumour is still listening to EGFR. The signal runs EGFR → RAS → RAF → MEK → ERK, and a KRAS mutation (most commonly G12C, G13, Q61) locks RAS in its active state, so it keeps sending signal without any push from upstream. Rectal cancer with a K-Ras mutation therefore does not respond to cetuximab; only K-Ras wild-type does, which makes this the cleanest example of a predictive biomarker deciding whether to use a drug. EGFR is the receptor itself, K-Ras is the stuck mutant driver gene, and daraxonrasib is the inhibitor aimed at RAS.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does a circulating surrogate marker refer to?
options: A foetal antigen, a blood marker that rises in colorectal cancer.
Using a cheap, easy-to-measure marker in place of the true endpoint you want to measure.
A surrogate marker that can be measured in blood.
His worked example in lecture three: integrating CNV copy number with mRNA expression to confirm that it is a driver.
questions.why: The reason it exists is very practical: to find out how big the tumour is, the standard method is a CT or MRI scan, which is expensive and cannot be done often; a blood marker is cheap, can be measured repeatedly, and can be used to track tumour burden. CEA is the most typical example — he uses it in colorectal cancer as a surrogate in place of repeated scans. CEA is one specific blood marker, surrogate endpoints is the concept of substituting a cheap, easy-to-measure marker for the true endpoint you want to measure, and NPM1 is his worked example from lecture three showing how to integrate CNV and mRNA expression to find a driver.

questions.q: Mutant K-Ras keeps sending signal without the upstream receptor firing; this state is called ____.
options: Constitutively active
GTP-bound
GAP-mediated GTP hydrolysis
Proliferative signal
questions.why: Normally a small G protein is activated only briefly when an upstream receptor (for example EGFR) fires, and then switches itself off. Mutant K-Ras is different: the mutation site (G12, G13, Q61) destroys its own 'off', GAP-promoted GTP hydrolysis fails, so Ras stays permanently in the GTP-bound active state and keeps sending growth and survival signals even when EGFR is silent — that is the true meaning of 'constitutively active', which is his 'car with the accelerator floored'. GTP-bound is the name of the active state, GAP-mediated GTP hydrolysis is the off switch that has been destroyed, and a proliferative signal is the message that starts the cell replicating its DNA.

questions.q: Which English term corresponds to 'the poisonous component on an ADC that does the killing'?
options: Small molecule
branched linker
Dual-payload ADC
cytotoxic payload
questions.why: The antibody is the 'delivery man' and the payload is the 'goods'. It has to satisfy two conditions at once: it must be highly toxic, killing the cell once inside; and it must be carried stably to the target and released there, otherwise it is released in the bloodstream first, the toxicity never reaches the tumour and normal cells are harmed instead. His examples are DNA-damaging payloads such as the topoisomerase inhibitors (SN-38, DXd). A small molecule is a drug-sized chemical molecule, a branched linker is the branched connector that carries two drugs at once, and a dual-payload ADC is the design that carries two drugs on the same antibody.

questions.q: In this course, Daraxonrasib (Rasonque) stands for which of the following?
options: A target that no drug can currently attack; K-Ras was formerly the most famous example.
A RAS inhibitor; median overall survival 13.2 months, against 6.7 months for chemotherapy.
Its stuck mutant form drives many cancers, including colorectal and pancreatic cancer.
Using the antibody as a delivery vehicle, carrying a toxic drug only to the place it recognises.
questions.why: RAS has long been called 'undruggable': it is a small GTPase that is active when bound to GTP and switches off when hydrolysed to GDP, and its surface has no obvious deep pocket into which a small molecule can dock. His lecture one quotes a mock FDA press release (26 August 2026): Rasonque (daraxonrasib) was approved for metastatic pancreatic cancer, with a trial enrolling 500 adults with previously treated pancreatic adenocarcinoma; median overall survival was 13.2 months against 6.7 months for standard chemotherapy. The point is that the 'undruggability' of K-Ras is a pharmacological difficulty, not a biological one. An undruggable target is the label K-Ras used to carry, K-Ras is the stuck mutant gene, and an ADC is the delivery platform that carries a poison on an antibody.

questions.q: Which drug name corresponds to 'an ADC targeting TROP2' in English?
options: trastuzumab-deruxtecan
SN-38
datopotamab-deruxtecan
Cetuximab
questions.why: The two clinical, marketed ADCs he names come as a pair, one matched to HER2 and one to TROP2: trastuzumab-deruxtecan is the one that targets HER2, and datopotamab-deruxtecan is the one that targets TROP2. Both carry payloads from the topoisomerase inhibitor family, and the only difference is which antigen the antibody recognises — the design logic is identical: deliver a topoisomerase inhibitor to the tumour's doorstep. SN-38 is the topoisomerase-I inhibitor payload on an ADC and cetuximab is an anti-EGFR antibody; neither of them targets TROP2.

questions.q: Which English term corresponds to 'the umbrella term for topoisomerase inhibitor payloads of the DXd type'?
options: deruxtecan
DXd
SN-38
Small molecule
questions.why: The deruxtecan family of molecules is a novel type of topoisomerase inhibitor used as the toxic part of an ADC. It causes DNA damage that stops cells replicating, so an ADC using it amounts to 'delivering a DNA-destroying tool to the tumour's doorstep'. The core reasoning of ADC design is that the antibody handles 'delivering' while the payload handles 'killing', and the payload's mechanism has to be offset from the tumour's resistance strategy. DXd is one specific payload code name, SN-38 is another topoisomerase-I inhibitor payload, and a small molecule means a drug-sized chemical molecule.

questions.q: In this course, which of the following does 'drug target' mean?
options: A membrane receptor with its own kinase activity; HER2 is one.
Compressing thousands of measurements into a few axes so that cells can be plotted as points.
The public database he uses to nominate drug targets and to find out where a protein is made.
The molecule a drug is designed to act on. Membrane proteins and kinases are the best examples.
questions.why: A molecule that can serve as a drug target has to satisfy three things at once: first, in patient data it must be specifically overexpressed in the disease; second, it must be structurally tractable, meaning there is a way for a small molecule, an antibody or a nucleic acid drug to get at it; third, the competitive landscape must not be too crowded. And 'disease-causing' is not the same as 'druggable': cytoskeletal components, for example, are crucial in metastasis yet are very hard to attack selectively; telomerase is a genuinely druggable example, with antisense oligonucleotides and small molecules in clinical trials. An RTK is a membrane receptor with kinase activity, PCA is the method that reduces thousands of measurements to fewer dimensions, and the Human Protein Atlas is the public database he uses to nominate targets.

questions.q: What does 'dual-payload ADC' refer to in this course?
options: Using the antibody as a delivery vehicle, carrying a toxic drug only to the place it recognises.
An ADC that carries two drugs on the same antibody.
A branched linker that carries two drugs at once.
The poisonous component on an ADC that does the killing.
questions.why: The approach is to replace the single linker with a branched linker that hangs two drugs side by side on the antibody: usually a topoisomerase inhibitor plus an inhibitor of the DNA damage response (for example an ATM blocker). The aim is to get round the resistance that a single payload generates — if the tumour resists only the first drug, the second still works. The cost is a bigger molecule and a lower drug payload, so this remains a research-stage design rather than an approved standard practice. The ADC itself is the delivery platform that carries a poison on an antibody, the branched linker is the forked connector, and the cytotoxic payload is the poisonous component that does the killing.

questions.q: Which code name corresponds to 'the drug payload carried by trastuzumab deruxtecan' in English?
options: deruxtecan
SN-38
DXd
Small molecule
questions.why: DXd is the code name for the deruxtecan topoisomerase I inhibitor payload; trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) attaches it to an anti-HER2 antibody with a linker. The logic of an ADC is to separate 'finding the tumour' from 'killing the cell': the antibody delivers the whole complex to the surface of cells with high HER2 expression, and only then is the payload released inside the cell to cause DNA damage. The same payload hung on a Trop2 antibody becomes datopotamab deruxtecan. Deruxtecan is the umbrella term for this class of payload, SN-38 is another topoisomerase-I inhibitor, and a small molecule means a drug-sized chemical molecule.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes EGFR in this course's signalling pathway and targeted therapy?
options: The growth factor receptor at the very top of the RAS chain. Blocking it is a standard anticancer drug strategy.
An anti-EGFR antibody; effective in K-Ras wild-type rectal cancer, ineffective in patients with K-Ras mutations.
A cell surface protein that is an antibody target in lung and breast cancer.
A membrane receptor with its own kinase activity; HER2 is one.
questions.why: EGFR is a receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) sitting at the very top of the growth signalling chain EGFR → RAS → RAF → MEK → ERK. Normally it is activated only when there is a ligand outside the cell; once activated it passes the phosphate group downwards, pushing RAS into its active Ras-GTP form. There are two drug strategies: an anti-EGFR antibody (cetuximab) that blocks the ligand at the receptor, or a small-molecule kinase inhibitor that suppresses the kinase activity directly. But the premise is that the downstream must be clean: if K-Ras itself mutates to become continuously active, blocking the receptor achieves nothing. Cetuximab is that antibody, Trop2 is another surface antigen, and RTK is the structural class of these receptors.

questions.q: What is he trying to show by using ERBB2 as an example?
options: The study of the chemical composition of exhaled breath, used to look inside the body.
Compressing thousands of measurements into a few axes so that cells can be plotted as points.
A cell surface protein that is an antibody target in lung and breast cancer.
The same target can point in opposite prognostic directions in different cancer types, so drug targets and prognostic biomarkers must be cancer-type specific.
questions.why: ERBB2 is the gene name for HER2 (human epidermal growth factor receptor 2); the two are the gene name and the protein name for the same thing. He used the ERBB2 page of the Human Protein Atlas for a key demonstration: the same target can point in completely opposite prognostic directions in different cancers — renal cancer is favourable, while endometrial cancer and pancreatic cancer are both unfavourable, all three at p < 0.001. The lesson is that drug targets and prognostic biomarkers must be cancer-type specific; you cannot generalise from one cancer type to another. The chemical composition of exhaled breath, the dimensionality reduction of PCA and the surface antigen Trop2 have nothing to do with this demonstration.

questions.q: The common filtering threshold on a volcano plot is p < 0.05 together with ____ , used to control false positives.
options: Metabolomics
FDR
PCA (principal component analysis)
Metabolite fingerprint
questions.why: When you test thousands of features at once, a batch of them will be 'significant' purely by luck. FDR acknowledges this: it estimates how many of the results you have called significant are in fact false, so the threshold commonly seen on a volcano plot is p < 0.05 together with FDR < 0.15. Drawing the p-value threshold and the FDR threshold on the volcano plot and taking their intersection controls false positives and excessive stringency at the same time. Metabolomics is the study of all the small molecules in a sample, PCA is the method that compresses thousands of measurements into a few axes, and a metabolite fingerprint is the small-molecule pattern of a sample.

questions.q: The G12, G13 and Q61 mutations in K-Ras destroy ____ , so Ras stays permanently in the GTP-bound active state.
options: GTP-bound
Constitutively active
GAP-mediated GTP hydrolysis
Proliferative signal
questions.why: Normally a small G protein is on when it is bound to GTP, but GTPase-activating protein (GAP) catalyses the hydrolysis of GTP to GDP, so the protein automatically returns to the off state. The G12, G13 and Q61 mutations of K-Ras destroy exactly this lever, so Ras stays permanently in the GTP-bound active state and keeps passing growth signals down; the easiest way to remember it is to think of GAP as the handbrake. GTP-bound is the name of the active state, constitutively active is this state of staying on without any upstream signal, and a proliferative signal is the message that starts the cell replicating its DNA.

questions.q: He uses GC-MS to analyse volatile substances in exhaled breath; what is the reason for this division of labour?
options: Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry: it first separates the chemicals in a sample, then identifies them.
Nuclear magnetic resonance: it is used to work out the shape of molecules in solution.
Compressing thousands of measurements into a few axes so that cells can be plotted as points.
The study of all the small molecules in a sample. Many biomarkers are found this way.
questions.why: GC-MS links two instruments together: gas chromatography (GC) does the separation — the sample is vaporised and injected onto a column, where the compounds separate according to their volatility and adsorption and elute one by one — while mass spectrometry (MS) does the identification, smashing each eluting compound into charged fragments by electron impact, arranging them into a mass spectrum by mass-to-charge ratio and matching that against a database to get a name. In the division of labour GC-MS suits molecules that are volatile and thermally stable, LC-MS suits those that are less volatile and larger, and NMR suits very high concentrations — and the VOCs in exhaled breath are exactly volatile substances, so they are measured by GC/MS. Nuclear magnetic resonance, the unsupervised dimensionality-reduction method and the field that studies all small molecules are not the reason for this division of labour.

questions.q: The first metabolic step that cuts one six-carbon glucose into two three-carbon pyruvates, entirely in the cytoplasm and without needing oxygen, is called ____ in English.
options: Warburg effect
Aerobic glycolysis
Lactate
Glycolysis
questions.why: Glycolysis is a ten-step reaction that takes place entirely in the cytoplasm without needing oxygen, netting 2 ATP and 2 NADH. What happens to pyruvate is decided by oxygen: with oxygen plentiful it enters the mitochondria and runs the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation for about 36 ATP in total; without oxygen lactate dehydrogenase turns it into lactate and only the 2 ATP are recovered. The Warburg effect is the aerobic glycolysis favoured by cancer cells, aerobic glycolysis is the name of that pathway, and lactate is the molecule produced by fermentation.

questions.q: The active state of a small G protein when it is bound to GTP is called ____ in English.
options: Constitutively active
GTP-bound
GAP-mediated GTP hydrolysis
Drug target
questions.why: A small G protein is like a plug: plugged into GTP (GTP-bound) the circuit is live, and with the plug pulled out and GDP in its place the circuit is dead; normally it goes live for a few seconds and then switches itself off, whereas mutant Ras is a plug that is stuck and cannot be pulled out, so the signal keeps flowing — grasp this and you grasp why a K-Ras mutation amounts to a floored accelerator. Constitutively active is the state of staying on without any upstream signal, GAP-mediated GTP hydrolysis is the small G protein's own off switch, and a drug target is the molecule a drug is designed to act on.

questions.q: In the biomarker workflow, what role does the Human Protein Atlas play?
options: The study of all the small molecules in a sample. Many biomarkers are found this way.
His worked example in lecture three: integrating CNV copy number with mRNA expression to confirm that it is a driver.
The public database he uses to nominate drug targets and to find out where a protein is made.
The study of the chemical composition of exhaled breath, used to look inside the body.
questions.why: The Human Protein Atlas is a public database of human protein expression recording, for every gene, which tissues express it, how much, and any prognostic association in specific cancers. He demonstrates with the ERBB2 page: the predicted location, 11 transcripts, an RNA category of low tissue specificity, a TCGA category of low cancer specificity, and — most importantly — the line prognostic marker in renal cancer (favourable), endometrial cancer (unfavourable) and pancreatic cancer (unfavourable), with all three KM curves at p < 0.001. In the biomarker workflow it plays the key 'checking and judging' step: confirming whether the protein is also expressed in normal tissue (which sets the therapeutic window) and whether it is associated with prognosis. Metabolomics is the field that studies all small molecules, NPM1 is the worked example integrating CNV and mRNA to find a driver, and breathomics is the technique that analyses exhaled breath.

questions.q: Which English term corresponds to 'its stuck mutant form drives many cancers, including colorectal and pancreatic cancer'?
options: K-Ras
BRAF
EGFR
Undraggable target
questions.why: Normal K-Ras is only a messenger: it switches to its active form only when upstream EGFR fires. The mutation stops GAP from hydrolysing its GTP, so it sticks in the 'on' position and keeps sending out both growth signals, RAF–MEK–ERK and PI3K–AKT–mTOR, whether or not there is an upstream signal. He also uses K-Ras to show how a predictive biomarker is used: cetuximab (anti-EGFR) fails in K-Ras mutant colorectal cancer because the receptor is blocked while the downstream is still lit up; KRAS G12C is found in 13% of lung adenocarcinoma and 3% of colorectal cancer. BRAF is the kinase downstream in the MAPK pathway, EGFR is the receptor at the very top of the signalling chain, and an undruggable target is the label K-Ras used to carry.

questions.q: Which English term corresponds to 'the step curve showing how patients' survival probability changes over time'?
options: Metabolite fingerprint
PCA (principal component analysis)
Drug target
Kaplan-Meier curve
questions.why: A KM curve is a step function assembled from the time at which each patient had an event: where someone dies or the disease progresses the curve steps down; a flat stretch means no events during that period; and the little tick marks on the curve are the censored patients. The point at which the curve crosses 0.5 is the median survival; two curves are compared with a log-rank test, and if they separate that means the two groups of patients can be told apart. A metabolite fingerprint is the small-molecule fingerprint of a sample, PCA is the method that reduces thousands of measurements to fewer dimensions, and a drug target is the molecule a drug is designed to act on.

questions.q: Which English term corresponds to 'the molecule produced when cancer cells ferment sugar instead of burning it'?
options: Metabolite
Lactate
Warburg effect
Glycolysis
questions.why: A normal cell with oxygen can make about 36 ATP from one glucose; a cancer cell instead sends about 85% of its pyruvate off to become lactate and lets only about 5% into the mitochondria, so the yield drops to about 4 ATP. It looks wasteful, but fermentation leaves the half-split sugar on the spot, and those intermediates are exactly the building material for nucleotides, lipids and amino acids. Metabolite is the large category of metabolic molecules, the Warburg effect is the name for this trade-off, and glycolysis is the process of cutting glucose into pyruvate.

questions.q: In this course, what does 'median overall survival' refer to?
options: Its stuck mutant form drives many cancers, including colorectal and pancreatic cancer.
A surrogate marker that can be measured in blood.
The median overall survival of a group of patients.
The step curve showing how patients' survival probability changes over time.
questions.why: This is the endpoint measure most often reported in clinical trials: a median means that half the patients live longer than it and half live less long. In the Rasonque (daraxonrasib) trial, in n = 500 previously treated patients with metastatic pancreatic cancer, median overall survival on the new drug was 13.2 months against 6.7 months for standard chemotherapy, roughly twice as long. The advantage of the median is that it is not swayed by extreme values; a mean, by contrast, can be pulled about by one or two patients who live unusually long or unusually briefly. K-Ras is the stuck mutant driver gene, a circulating surrogate marker is a surrogate measured in blood, and the Kaplan-Meier curve is the step curve showing how survival probability changes over time.

questions.q: Which English term corresponds to 'a small molecule made or consumed when cells work'?
options: Metabolite
Metabolomics
Metabolite fingerprint
Lactate
questions.why: Metabolites are the intermediates and end products of metabolism: glucose, pyruvate, lactate and acetyl-CoA all belong to the list. They are ideal objects for biomarkers because they reflect the state of the cell at this moment rather than its genomic potential: the same patient may have identical genes and completely different metabolites, so the disease acquires a chemical fingerprint. Metabolomics is the study of all the small molecules in a sample, a metabolite fingerprint is the pattern of small molecules that makes one sample differ from another, and lactate is one specific metabolite among them.

questions.q: What does 'metabolite fingerprint' mean in this course's metabolomics workflow?
options: Compressing thousands of measurements into a few axes so that cells can be plotted as points.
The study of all the small molecules in a sample. Many biomarkers are found this way.
A small molecule made or consumed when cells work.
The pattern of small molecules that makes one sample different from another.
questions.why: Measuring all the metabolites in a sample at once yields a compositional fingerprint; line up the fingerprints of several samples and compress them with PCA into a few axes, and you can see which samples cluster together and which are outliers. Differential metabolites are screened with a volcano plot (cut-off p < 0.05 and FDR < 0.15), then intersected with VIP > 1.0. He does not actually use this name; what it corresponds to is the result of step five of his seven-step metabolomics workflow, 'feature extraction → multivariate stats → PCA → heatmap'. PCA is the dimensionality-reduction method, metabolomics is the study of all small molecules, and a metabolite is the small molecule itself.

questions.q: He stresses that a biomarker only counts once it has been validated; how is this put into practice in the metabolomics workflow?
options: The study of the chemical composition of exhaled breath, used to look inside the body.
The whole workflow squeezes thousands of small molecules down to a few verifiable candidates, and multi-centre validation is what establishes the candidates.
Using a cheap, easy-to-measure marker in place of the true endpoint you want to measure.
The median overall survival of a group of patients.
questions.why: His workflow has seven steps: experimental design (a cohort plus animal experiments), sample collection (urine, blood and cerebrospinal fluid, tissue), sample pre-processing (homogenisation, liquid–liquid or solid-phase extraction, centrifugation), instrumental analysis (NMR, GC-MS, LC-MS), data mining (feature extraction, multivariate statistics, PCA, heatmap), biomarker discovery (volcano plot plus Venn diagram) and multi-centre validation. The screening criteria are p < 0.05 and FDR < 0.15, after which a Venn diagram picks out the differential metabolites that also satisfy VIP > 1.0; the point of the whole workflow is to squeeze thousands of small molecules down to a few candidates that can be validated. The chemical composition of exhaled breath is a different application branch, surrogate endpoints means substituting a cheap marker for the true endpoint, and median overall survival is the endpoint measure of a clinical trial.

questions.q: Of the three main instruments in metabolomics, what role does NMR play?
options: Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry: it first separates the chemicals in a sample, then identifies them.
The study of all the small molecules in a sample. Many biomarkers are found this way.
Nuclear magnetic resonance: it is used to work out the shape of molecules in solution.
Compressing thousands of measurements into a few axes so that cells can be plotted as points.
questions.why: Atomic nuclei align in a magnetic field: put the sample in the field, perturb it with radiofrequency pulses and listen to the signal from the nuclei, where different chemical environments give different shifts and the molecular structure can be worked back out; it does not require the sample to be separated or derivatised first and it is non-destructive. In the division of labour, GC-MS suits molecules that are volatile and thermally stable, LC-MS suits those that are less volatile and larger, and NMR suits very high concentrations. GC-MS separates first and identifies second, metabolomics is the whole research field, and PCA is the method that reduces thousands of measurements to fewer dimensions.

questions.q: What is the NPM1 example in his lecture three meant to demonstrate?
options: You have to integrate CNV copy number with mRNA expression: only a gene whose copy number has increased and whose transcriptional expression has risen in step can really be a driver that confers a growth advantage.
Compressing thousands of measurements into a few axes so that cells can be plotted as points.
The step curve showing how patients' survival probability changes over time.
Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry: it first separates the chemicals in a sample, then identifies them.
questions.why: The real use of this entry is to teach how to find a driver: only a gene whose copy number has increased and whose transcriptional expression has risen in step can really confer a growth advantage; looking at mutations alone or copy number alone is not enough. NPM1 appears in the heatmap and the PPI network in his lecture three, and NPM1-high patients also differ in overall survival and cumulative relapse. He is explicit that the molecular mechanism of CNV is offered only as 'a taste' and that there is no need to be frightened of those mechanisms. PCA's dimensionality reduction, the Kaplan-Meier step curve and GC-MS analysis are not what this lecture is demonstrating.

questions.q: Which English term corresponds to 'a gene that drives cell division once it has been switched on too far, a driver after mutation'?
options: Drug target
Predictive biomarker
Prognostic biomarker
Oncogene
questions.why: A normal gene is a brake or an accelerator; an oncogene is a jammed accelerator: genes such as K-Ras and HER2, once they are made continuously active by mutation, amplification or translocation, send the cell a 'keep growing' signal. In contrast to a tumour-suppressor gene, the problem with an oncogene is not loss of function but the inability to switch off, so a drug can go straight at the switch that stays permanently on. In lecture one he uses K-Ras to illustrate the 'stuck switch', and he also lists driver and passenger as a common pairing in multiple-choice questions. A drug target is the molecule a drug is designed to act on, a predictive biomarker predicts treatment response, and a prognostic biomarker describes the natural history of the disease.

questions.q: In this course's metabolomics workflow, what does PCA do?
options: The study of all the small molecules in a sample. Many biomarkers are found this way.
Compressing thousands of measurements into a few axes so that cells can be plotted as points.
The pattern of small molecules that makes one sample different from another.
A small molecule made or consumed when cells work.
questions.why: When thousands of genes are measured at once, each sample is a point in several thousand dimensions and cannot be plotted. PCA finds the few directions that 'explain the variance best' and projects the points onto those few axes, so that clustering becomes visible: which group of points clusters together (possibly a cell type) and which points are outliers (possibly an abnormal sample). It is an unsupervised method; it does not give you the answer, it only makes the structure visible. He lists PCA at step five of the metabolomics workflow, data mining, and shows the grouping of different cell types with a t-SNE plot. Metabolomics is the study of all small molecules, a metabolite fingerprint is the small-molecule pattern of a sample, and a metabolite is the small molecule itself.

questions.q: When HER2 is bound by Herceptin and can no longer pair with HER3, the downstream ____ is not activated, so the cell's survival signal is cut off.
options: EGFR
Receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK)
PI3K
Trop2
questions.why: PI3K has two subunits, p85 and p110; it is his example of explaining to beginners the chain running from 'the receptor is blocked by the drug → the downstream signal goes out'. Downstream of PI3K lies a whole series of messages promoting growth and survival, so blocking the upstream receptor is equivalent to turning the volume of the entire downstream cascade back to zero. EGFR is the receptor at the very top of the signalling chain, receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) is the structural class of these receptors, and Trop2 is another surface antigen target.

questions.q: In the case from lecture one, K-Ras status is treated as a predictive biomarker; what does that mean?
options: It answers 'which drug works for this patient': cetuximab (anti-EGFR) fails in mutant colorectal cancer because the downstream signal is still lit up, so K-Ras status is a marker predicting that the drug will not work.
A marker that tells you how the disease will behave whatever treatment you give.
The gene name for HER2.
A foetal antigen, a blood marker that rises in colorectal cancer.
questions.why: The question a predictive biomarker answers is 'which drug works for this patient'. The clearest example is K-Ras: cetuximab (anti-EGFR) fails in mutant colorectal cancer because the downstream signal is still lit up; so here K-Ras status is a marker predicting that the drug will not work, rather than a marker predicting that the disease will be worse. Being able to tell these two kinds of marker apart is the key to clinical decisions. A prognostic biomarker describes the natural history of the disease, ERBB2 is the gene name for HER2, and CEA is the blood marker of colorectal cancer.

questions.q: Which English term corresponds to 'a marker that tells you how the disease will behave whatever treatment you give'?
options: Predictive biomarker
circulating surrogate marker
surrogate endpoints
Prognostic biomarker
questions.why: It answers the question of the natural history of the disease, independent of treatment. The same marker can be prognostic in some cancer types and predictive in others: ERBB2 is favourable in renal cancer and unfavourable in endometrial and pancreatic cancer, yet only breast and gastric cancer show a clear survival benefit from anti-HER2 therapy; in other words, high expression does not mean 'this patient should get that drug'. A predictive biomarker predicts treatment response, a circulating surrogate marker is a surrogate measured in blood, and surrogate endpoints means substituting a cheap, easy-to-measure marker for the true endpoint you want to measure.

questions.q: In this course's signalling diagram, three pathways such as PI3K–AKT–mTOR and RAF–MEK–ERK all converge on the same endpoint; what is it?
options: Remaining switched on without any upstream signal.
The signal that tells the cell to start replicating its DNA.
GAP-promoted GTP hydrolysis, the small G protein's own off switch.
The active state of a small G protein when it is bound to GTP.
questions.why: Starting with a mitogen binding a membrane receptor, the signal runs all the way down: PI(4,5)P is cleaved by phospholipase C into DAG and IP3, and DAG activates PKC; PI3K activates AKT and mTOR in turn; and RTK runs RAF–MEK–ERK. The common end point is that Cyclin D–CDK4/6 phosphorylates pRb, E2F is released, and the cell cycle moves from G1 into S phase — all three pathways converge on the same end point that starts the cell replicating its DNA, and that is the proliferative signal. Constitutively active is the state of being stuck on and unable to switch off, GAP-mediated GTP hydrolysis is the small G protein's off switch, and GTP-bound is the name of the active state.

questions.q: Which English term corresponds to 'a membrane receptor with its own kinase activity; HER2 is one'?
options: EGFR
Trop2
Receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK)
PI3K
questions.why: The structure of an RTK is 'a receptor body that crosses the cell membrane' plus 'an intracellular kinase region'. Two receptors lock together through their extracellular ligand-binding domains (dimerisation), and each one's intracellular kinase then phosphorylates the other, passing the signal downstream; in a normal cell this route is a growth switch, while in a tumour it is a runaway growth engine. The key detail is that a monomer binds DNA poorly and dimerisation greatly increases affinity — and HER2 is precisely unable to dimerise efficiently with itself, forming heterodimers with HER1, HER3 and HER4 instead. EGFR is one of the receptors at the top of this chain, Trop2 is another surface protein, and PI3K is the kinase downstream of the receptor.

questions.q: A drug with a molecular weight below about 500 Da, well absorbed orally, able to fit into a receptor pocket or an enzyme active site, is called ____ in English.
options: Small molecule
Receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK)
cytotoxic payload
SN-38
questions.why: The definition of a small molecule is not the loose 'it's a small molecule' but an operable boundary: usually a molecular weight below about 500 Da, good oral absorption, and able to fit into a receptor pocket or an enzyme active site. Its advantages are that it is cheap, can be synthesised in bulk and is easy to design against structurally; its weaknesses are poor selectivity, since it readily hits several targets. By contrast, antibodies (biologics) are far larger and highly selective, but usually have to be injected and cannot be taken orally. He also uses it to explain the logic of an ADC: attaching a small molecule such as a topoisomerase inhibitor to an antibody so that it is delivered only to the tumour. Receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) is the structural class of membrane receptors, a cytotoxic payload is the poison on an ADC that does the killing, and SN-38 is one such topoisomerase-I inhibitor payload.

questions.q: What role does SN-38 play in this course?
options: A cell surface protein that is an antibody target in lung and breast cancer.
Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry: it first separates the chemicals in a sample, then identifies them.
The drug payload carried by trastuzumab deruxtecan.
A topoisomerase-I inhibitor used as the cytotoxic payload of an ADC.
questions.why: SN-38 is a topoisomerase I inhibitor: it prevents the tangle unwound ahead of the DNA replication fork from being re-ligated, so double-strand breaks accumulate in the DNA and the cell dies. The benefit of using it in an ADC is selective delivery — on its own it kills every dividing cell, whereas attached to an antibody it goes only to the targeted tumour. The clinical ADCs he names are trastuzumab-deruxtecan against HER2 and datopotamab-deruxtecan against TROP2, both carrying payloads from the topoisomerase inhibitor family. DXd is the code name of the payload carried by T-DXd, Trop2 is another surface antigen target, and GC-MS is the analytical instrument.

questions.q: In a clinical trial, substituting repeatedly measurable blood CEA for repeated CT scans is the practice of using ____ .
options: circulating surrogate marker
surrogate endpoints
median overall survival
Prognostic biomarker
questions.why: A trial's true endpoint might be how long patients survive or how big the tumour is, but both require scans, blood draws and waiting. A circulating biomarker (for example CEA) offers a surrogate that can be measured often and that tracks tumour burden, so the trial can read out a response without scanning every patient repeatedly. For a surrogate to stand up it must first be shown to move in step with the true endpoint; CEA is usable precisely because it broadly follows tumour burden. The concept of a circulating surrogate marker is a surrogate measured in blood, median overall survival is the true endpoint commonly reported in trials, and a prognostic biomarker is independent of treatment and describes the natural history of the disease.

questions.q: In this course, what class of drug does trastuzumab-deruxtecan belong to?
options: An anti-EGFR antibody; effective in K-Ras wild-type rectal cancer, ineffective in patients with K-Ras mutations.
An ADC targeting TROP2.
An ADC targeting HER2.
A RAS inhibitor; median overall survival 13.2 months, against 6.7 months for chemotherapy.
questions.why: Trastuzumab-deruxtecan is made up of the antibody trastuzumab linked to a topoisomerase inhibitor payload (DXd). It uses a DNA-damaging payload because if a tumour becomes resistant to a single drug, switching the mechanism of action can still work. The clinical ADC targets he currently names are two, HER2 and TROP2: one matched to trastuzumab-deruxtecan and one to datopotamab-deruxtecan. Cetuximab is an anti-EGFR antibody, datopotamab-deruxtecan is the one matched to TROP2, and daraxonrasib is the inhibitor aimed at RAS.

questions.q: Which English term corresponds to 'a cell surface protein that is an antibody target in lung and breast cancer'?
options: Trop2
ERBB2
EGFR
Receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK)
questions.why: Trop2 is a protein on the surface of epithelial cells, expressed at high levels in many solid tumours (breast cancer, lung cancer and so on), which makes it a suitable antibody target. The concept of an ADC is that the antibody delivers the cell close to the target while the payload kills the cell; the example for Trop2 is datopotamab-deruxtecan, alongside the HER2-targeting trastuzumab-deruxtecan, and both carry topoisomerase inhibitor payloads. ERBB2 is the gene name for HER2, EGFR is the receptor at the very top of the signalling chain, and receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) is the structural class of these receptors.

questions.q: In this course, what does 'undruggable target' refer to?
options: The molecule a drug is designed to act on. Membrane proteins and kinases are the best examples.
Its stuck mutant form drives many cancers, including colorectal and pancreatic cancer.
A RAS inhibitor; median overall survival 13.2 months, against 6.7 months for chemotherapy.
A target that no drug can currently attack; K-Ras was formerly the most famous example.
questions.why: 'Undruggable' has three distinct obstacles: first, there is no binding pocket to speak of (as with K-Ras, whose GTP-binding surface is smooth); second, the protein is indispensable in normal cells too, so selectivity is impossible (as with the cytoskeleton, which is crucial in metastasis, making it very hard to attack only the tumour's copy); third, there is not enough structural information to design a molecule. K-Ras was long regarded as undruggable until the example he mentions in lecture one: on 26 August 2026 the FDA approved Rasonque (daraxonrasib), a RAS inhibitor, for metastatic pancreatic cancer, with median overall survival of 13.2 against 6.7 months in the trial. A drug target is a druggable molecule, K-Ras is that gene, and daraxonrasib is the inhibitor aimed at it.

questions.q: Which of the following is the Warburg effect as described in this course?
options: The step curve showing how patients' survival probability changes over time.
Cancer cells fermenting glucose into lactate even in the presence of oxygen, because what they want is raw material, not fuel.
The first step of energy production: glucose is broken down into pyruvate without using oxygen.
The median overall survival of a group of patients.
questions.why: His lecture one slides set three situations side by side: a resting cell with oxygen makes about 36 ATP per glucose; without oxygen it makes only 2; and a proliferating cancer cell runs aerobic glycolysis whether or not oxygen is present, about 4, because it sends 85% of its pyruvate to lactate and leaves only about 5% for the mitochondria. The inefficiency is a matter of strategy: half-broken-down sugar molecules are ideal building material for nucleotides, lipids and amino acids, and a cell about to divide a billion times needs building material far more than it needs fuel. Glycolysis is the process of cutting glucose into pyruvate, median overall survival is the endpoint measure of a trial, and the Kaplan-Meier curve is the step curve of survival probability.
